objectives: Compare the composition, advantages, and controversies of dental amalgam, composite resin, and glass-ionomer cement.
Explain acid-etch bonding and adhesive dentistry from Buonocore's 1955 discovery to modern dentin adhesives.
Describe indirect restorations — inlays, onlays, and crowns — and the properties of modern dental ceramics.

slides.title: Direct restorative materials — amalgam, composite, and glass-ionomer
slides.body:
**Restorative dentistry** repairs teeth damaged by caries, fracture, or wear. **Direct restorations** are shaped inside the prepared cavity in a single visit; three materials dominate this category.

**Dental amalgam** is the oldest modern filling material, popularised by **G.V. Black**, who in the 1890s formulated a balanced alloy. Amalgam is made by triturating a powdered alloy — chiefly **silver (Ag), tin (Sn), and copper (Cu)**, sometimes with zinc — with liquid **mercury (Hg)**, which makes up roughly **43–50% of the set mass**. The mercury wets the alloy particles and the mass hardens through the formation of intermetallic phases (the silver–mercury **gamma-1 phase** and the tin–mercury **gamma-2 phase**; modern **high-copper amalgams** eliminate the weaker, corrosion-prone gamma-2 phase). Amalgam is strong, durable, cheap, and technique-tolerant, but it is silver-grey, requires removal of healthy tooth structure for mechanical retention, and is the subject of a long **mercury controversy**. Although the WHO and major dental associations regard set amalgam as safe for most patients, environmental concerns about mercury led to the **Minamata Convention on Mercury (2013)**, which calls for a global "phase-down" of amalgam use.

**Composite resin** is the tooth-coloured workhorse of modern dentistry. It is a **dimethacrylate polymer matrix** — classically based on **Bis-GMA (bisphenol A-glycidyl methacrylate)**, developed by **Rafael Bowen** at the National Bureau of Standards around **1962** — reinforced with **inorganic filler particles** (silica, glass, or zirconia) and bonded by a **silane coupling agent**. Composites are **light-cured**: a blue light (around **450–470 nm** from an LED curing unit) activates a **photoinitiator** such as **camphorquinone**, triggering free-radical polymerisation that sets the material on demand. Composites bond to tooth structure (see next slide), are aesthetic, and conserve tooth tissue, but they undergo **polymerisation shrinkage** and are more technique-sensitive.

**Glass-ionomer cement (GIC)**, invented by **Alan Wilson and Brian Kent in 1969** at the Laboratory of the Government Chemist in the UK, sets by an **acid–base reaction** between a fluoroaluminosilicate glass powder and a polyacrylic acid liquid. Its defining virtues are **chemical adhesion to enamel and dentin** without a separate bonding step and the **sustained release of fluoride**, which helps protect the surrounding tooth. GICs are weaker and less aesthetic than composite, so they are favoured for cervical lesions, liners, and high-caries-risk patients; **resin-modified glass ionomers (RMGI)** add a light-cured resin component for improved strength.

slides.title: Acid-etch bonding and the rise of adhesive dentistry
slides.body:
The single most transformative idea in restorative dentistry is **adhesive bonding** — the ability to glue restorations to the tooth rather than merely wedging them in. The breakthrough came from **Michael Buonocore**, who in **1955** published a paper in the *Journal of Dental Research* showing that treating enamel with **phosphoric acid** dramatically increased the adhesion of acrylic resins. This **acid-etch technique** works by selectively dissolving the enamel surface to create microscopic porosities into which fluid resin flows and locks, forming **resin tags** — a **micromechanical bond**.

Enamel bonding was reliable from the start, but **dentin bonding** proved far harder because dentin is wet, living, and rich in collagen. Etching dentin removes the **smear layer** (the debris created by cutting) and exposes a network of collagen fibrils and open dentinal tubules. The Japanese researcher **Nobuo Nakabayashi** described in **1982** the **hybrid layer** — a zone where adhesive resin infiltrates the demineralised collagen meshwork and polymerises in place, intertwining resin with tooth structure. Reliable dentin adhesives followed, evolving through several "generations":

- **Total-etch (etch-and-rinse)** systems apply phosphoric acid to both enamel and dentin, then rinse, then apply primer and adhesive. They give excellent enamel bonds but are sensitive to dentin over-drying.
- **Self-etch** systems use acidic primers that etch and prime simultaneously without a separate rinse, reducing technique sensitivity and post-operative sensitivity.
- **Universal (multi-mode) adhesives** can be used in either mode and often include the monomer **10-MDP**, which forms stable chemical bonds to calcium in hydroxyapatite as well as to zirconia.

The components of a modern adhesive include an **etchant** (phosphoric acid), a **primer** (hydrophilic monomers such as HEMA that wet the dentin), and a **bonding resin** (hydrophobic monomers that co-polymerise with the composite). The strength of a bond is often reported as **shear bond strength** in megapascals (MPa); good contemporary adhesives achieve **20–35 MPa** to enamel and dentin. Adhesive dentistry made possible the entire modern philosophy of **minimally invasive, tooth-conserving restoration**, replacing Black's principle of "extension for prevention" with the maxim "preserve and bond."

slides.title: Indirect restorations — inlays, onlays, crowns, and ceramics
slides.body:
When a tooth is too damaged for a direct filling, the dentist uses an **indirect restoration**, fabricated outside the mouth (in a laboratory or by a milling machine) from an impression or digital scan and then cemented in place. These range in coverage:

- An **inlay** fits within the cusps, replacing the inner part of the tooth (similar to a Class I or II filling but fabricated indirectly).
- An **onlay** covers one or more **cusp tips**, restoring greater structure while preserving more tooth than a full crown.
- A **crown** (cap) covers the entire clinical crown, used when so much tooth is lost — for example after root-canal treatment or a large fracture — that complete coverage is needed for strength.

Indirect restorations can be made from **gold alloys** (extremely durable and kind to opposing teeth, the historic gold standard), **porcelain-fused-to-metal (PFM)** (a metal coping for strength with a porcelain veneer for aesthetics), or, increasingly, **all-ceramic** materials. The materials science of dental ceramics has advanced rapidly:

- **Feldspathic porcelain** and **leucite-reinforced glass-ceramics** (such as **IPS Empress**) are highly aesthetic but relatively weak, suited to veneers and anterior crowns.
- **Lithium disilicate** (marketed as **IPS e.max**, introduced by **Ivoclar Vivadent** around 2005) is a glass-ceramic with flexural strength near **360–400 MPa**, combining good strength with translucency, widely used for crowns, inlays, and veneers.
- **Zirconia** (yttria-stabilised tetragonal zirconia polycrystal, **Y-TZP**) is the strongest dental ceramic, with flexural strength of **900–1200 MPa**, exploiting a toughening mechanism called **transformation toughening** in which crack-tip stress triggers a phase change that resists crack propagation. Early zirconia was opaque, suited to posterior crowns and bridge frameworks; newer **translucent multilayer zirconia** is aesthetic enough for anterior use.

Ceramics are bonded with **resin cements**, often after etching the fitting surface — silica-based ceramics with **hydrofluoric acid** and silane, and zirconia with **10-MDP-containing primers** since it cannot be acid-etched. The choice among these materials balances **strength, aesthetics, tooth conservation, and cost** — the central trade-off of restorative practice, and one increasingly executed with the digital CAD/CAM workflows examined in a later lesson.

question.question: Roughly what proportion of set dental amalgam is mercury, and which international agreement calls for phasing down its use?
options: About 43–50% mercury; the Minamata Convention on Mercury (2013).
Amalgam contains no mercury; the Basel Convention.
question.explanation: Dental amalgam is roughly 43–50% mercury by mass, alloyed with silver, tin, and copper. The Minamata Convention on Mercury (2013) targets a global phase-down of amalgam use for environmental reasons. The Kyoto and Montreal Protocols concern greenhouse gases and ozone-depleting substances respectively, and amalgam definitely contains mercury, so option D is false.

hints: Nearly half of set amalgam is the liquid metal that binds the alloy.
The treaty is named after a Japanese bay associated with mercury poisoning.
slides.workedSolution: Dental amalgam is produced by mixing a silver–tin–copper alloy powder with liquid mercury, which constitutes roughly 43–50% of the final set mass and forms the intermetallic phases that harden the filling. Although set amalgam is considered safe for most patients by major health bodies, mercury is an environmental pollutant, and the 2013 Minamata Convention on Mercury commits signatories to a phase-down of amalgam, accelerating the shift toward composite and other alternatives.

question.question: What did Michael Buonocore demonstrate in 1955 that founded adhesive dentistry?
options: That mercury could be safely removed from amalgam.
That treating enamel with phosphoric acid greatly increases resin adhesion via micromechanical retention.
That zirconia could be etched with hydrofluoric acid.
That fluoride could be released from glass-ionomer cement.
question.explanation: Buonocore's 1955 paper showed that etching enamel with phosphoric acid creates microporosities into which resin flows and locks, the micromechanical basis of all modern bonding. Mercury removal (A), zirconia etching (C — zirconia in fact cannot be acid-etched), and GIC fluoride release (D, Wilson and Kent 1969) are unrelated to Buonocore's contribution.

hints: Think about acid creating microscopic roughness on enamel.
The acid is phosphoric acid, applied to enamel.
slides.workedSolution: In 1955 Michael Buonocore published in the Journal of Dental Research that pre-treating enamel with phosphoric acid markedly increased the adhesion of acrylic resin. The acid selectively dissolves the enamel surface to produce microscopic porosities; liquid resin penetrates these and hardens into resin tags, creating a strong micromechanical bond. This acid-etch technique is the foundation of adhesive dentistry, later extended to dentin via Nakabayashi's hybrid-layer concept, and it underpins tooth-coloured composite restorations and ceramic bonding.

question.question: Lithium disilicate has a flexural strength of about 400 MPa, while yttria-stabilised zirconia has about 1200 MPa. How many times stronger (by this measure) is zirconia than lithium disilicate? Give a whole number.
question.hint: Divide the zirconia value by the lithium disilicate value: $1200 / 400$.

question.question: Which property most distinguishes glass-ionomer cement and makes it useful in high-caries-risk patients?
options: It is the strongest restorative material available.
It chemically bonds to tooth structure and releases fluoride over time.
It is cured exclusively by ultraviolet light at 365 nm.
question.explanation: Glass-ionomer cement (Wilson and Kent, 1969) sets by an acid–base reaction, bonds chemically to enamel and dentin without a separate adhesive, and releases fluoride that helps protect the adjacent tooth — valuable where caries risk is high. It is weaker than composite (A is false), conventional GIC sets chemically rather than by UV (C), and it contains no mercury (D).

hints: Two signature features: chemical adhesion and an ion that fights decay.
slides.workedSolution: Glass-ionomer cement is formed from a fluoroaluminosilicate glass powder and a polyacrylic acid liquid that react in an acid–base setting reaction. Two properties set it apart: it bonds chemically to enamel and dentin without needing a separate etch-and-bond step, and it slowly releases fluoride into the surrounding tooth, providing local anti-caries protection. These make GIC especially useful for cervical lesions, cavity liners, and patients with high caries risk, even though it is weaker and less aesthetic than composite resin.

question.question: Choosing a restoration for a heavily broken-down molar after root canal
question.prompt: A patient has a lower first molar that has just completed root-canal treatment and has lost both the mesial and distal walls plus a cusp, leaving thin remaining tooth structure. The patient is concerned about both strength and appearance and asks whether a large composite filling would suffice or whether a crown is needed. Drawing on the trade-offs among direct composite, onlays, and full crowns, and the properties of lithium disilicate versus zirconia, explain what you would recommend, why coverage of the cusps matters for a root-treated tooth, and how the material choice balances strength against aesthetics.
